title: Measure and record well
text: Choose an instrument with a suitable range and resolution for the variable. Record mass, volume, time, temperature, length, pH, current and potential difference with units and appropriate precision. Distinguish resolution from a guaranteed measurement accuracy.
points: Record raw readings immediately and include instrument uncertainty where appropriate.
Read liquid volumes at eye level; select a volumetric pipette or flask for accurate fixed volumes.
Calibrate or zero instruments and control environmental conditions.
example: Example: a 25.00 cm³ pipette with stated ±0.03 cm³ uncertainty gives a percentage uncertainty of (0.03/25.00) × 100 = 0.12%.

title: Standard solutions and dilutions
text: To prepare a standard solution, weigh a known amount of a suitable solute, dissolve it, transfer it quantitatively to a volumetric flask and make up to the mark. Dilution conserves the amount of solute transferred, so C₁V₁ = C₂V₂.
points: Rinse all transferred solute into the flask; dissolve before making up to volume.
Use a pipette for a precise aliquot; use a volumetric flask for final volume.
Stopper and invert to mix thoroughly.
example: Example: dilute 25.0 cm³ of 0.200 mol dm⁻³ solution to 100.0 cm³. C₂ = 0.200 × 25.0/100.0 = 0.0500 mol dm⁻³.

title: Titration and equivalence
text: A titration measures the quantity of one reactant needed to react with a known sample of another. Read the burette at the beginning and end; their difference is the titre. An indicator endpoint approximates the equivalence point but is not its definition.
points: Use a pipette to transfer a known sample volume to the flask.
Repeat measurements to obtain consistent titres; justify data selection.
Use the balanced equation to convert moles of titrant to moles of sample.
example: Example: 20.00 cm³ of 0.1000 mol dm⁻³ NaOH neutralizes 25.00 cm³ HCl. n(NaOH) = 0.002000 mol, so [HCl] = 0.002000/0.02500 = 0.08000 mol dm⁻³.

title: Separation and purification
text: Choose a technique from relevant physical properties. Filtration separates insoluble solids; recrystallization exploits changing solubility; distillation exploits volatility. Reflux heats a reaction while returning condensed vapour to the vessel instead of collecting it.
points: Know paper/TLC chromatography and how to measure Rf.
Use melting point determination to help evaluate purity.
Dry to constant mass by repeating drying, cooling and weighing until the mass is unchanged within the relevant precision.
example: Example: Rf = 2.4 cm / 6.0 cm = 0.40. A lower Rf in the same chromatographic system suggests relatively greater attraction to the stationary phase.

title: Energy, cells and light measurements
text: Calorimetry estimates heat from a temperature change. Electrochemical cells connect oxidation and reduction half-cells. Colorimetry or spectrophotometry measures how a sample interacts with light and can use calibration data to determine concentration.
points: Insulate calorimetry apparatus and evaluate heat loss and heat capacity assumptions.
Distinguish anode, cathode and charge carriers in electrochemical setups.
Use a suitable blank and calibration series for optical measurements; use physical or digital models to explore molecular structure.
example: Example: 100.0 g solution warms by 3.0 K. With c = 4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹, q = mcΔT = 1254 J. Assess whether ignored heat loss would change the inferred reaction enthalpy.

title: Technology and data sources
text: Use sensors, databases, simulations and computer models to collect data. Use spreadsheets to process data and present graphs. Distinguish real measurements from outputs generated by an assumed model.
points: Check the source, measurement conditions, units and reliability of database values.
Use spreadsheet formulas consistently, then inspect outputs for unit or reference errors.
Explain assumptions and limits when using simulations or molecular models.
example: Example: record a sensor temperature series with timestamps and graph temperature against time. Identify the measured trend before fitting a model.

title: Maths, significant figures and units
text: Apply arithmetic, algebra, ratios, logarithms, scientific notation, rates of change and proportionality. HL also includes exponential functions. Express values and uncertainties at precision that reflects the data, rather than every calculator digit.
points: Use SI units and prefixes; convert volumes and temperatures before substitution.
Distinguish percentage change, percentage difference and percentage error.
Estimate order of magnitude to detect implausible results.
example: Example: relative error for an experimental value 9.8 and accepted value 10.0 is |9.8 − 10.0|/10.0 × 100 = 2.0%.

title: Uncertainty propagation
text: An uncertainty describes a range of plausible measurement values. For the IB additive rules, add absolute uncertainties in sums or differences, and add fractional or percentage uncertainties in products or quotients. For powers at HL, multiply the relative uncertainty by the magnitude of the exponent.
points: Quote raw readings and uncertainty consistently in units and decimal places.
Distinguish absolute, fractional and percentage uncertainty.
Avoid implying that uncertainty alone proves a particular source of systematic error.
example: Example: A = 5.0 ± 0.1 and B = 2.0 ± 0.1. A − B = 3.0 ± 0.2. For A/B, percentage uncertainty ≈ 2% + 5% = 7%, giving 2.5 ± 0.2 after sensible rounding.

title: Graphing and interpreting evidence
text: Use graphs to reveal relationships, not simply to decorate data. Label axes with quantity and units, select suitable scales, show uncertainty bars and fit an appropriate line or curve. Read gradients, intercepts, extrema and changes of slope in the scientific context.
points: Distinguish interpolation from extrapolation; the latter has additional uncertainty.
Use R² to assess model fit while checking residual patterns and the model itself.
Distinguish correlation from a causal explanation; justify handling of outliers.
example: Example: for a straight-line concentration–time segment, rate is obtained from gradient Δc/Δt. State whether the sign denotes disappearance or appearance.

title: Design a valid investigation
text: Frame a focused research question linking an independent variable to a measurable dependent variable in a defined system. Use scientific understanding to predict a relationship and design a method that can test it fairly.
points: Identify and justify independent, dependent and control variables.
Choose a sufficient range, repetitions and quantity of measurements; pilot the method.
Address specific safety, ethical and environmental issues; justify calibration, insulation and environmental controls.
example: Example: instead of “Does temperature affect rate?”, define the reaction, temperature range, rate measurement and fixed concentrations, then explain how the design isolates temperature.

title: Collect, conclude and evaluate
text: Record sufficient quantitative data and relevant qualitative observations, process them accurately and use them to answer the research question. Compare conclusions with accepted scientific context and explain how uncertainty affects confidence.
points: Differentiate accuracy, precision, reliability and validity.
Explain the impact of random errors, systematic errors, assumptions and limitations.
Propose realistic improvements tied to specific effects rather than “use better equipment”.
example: Example: heat loss in calorimetry can reduce the observed ΔT and make a measured exothermic enthalpy too small in magnitude. Better insulation addresses this specific systematic limitation.

title: Scientific investigation and assessment
tag: IA · Same requirements at SL and HL
text: The uploaded guide allocates 20% of the final assessment to a scientific investigation, with a report of up to 3,000 words and approximately 10 hours. The four criteria are Research design, Data analysis, Conclusion and Evaluation, each worth six marks. The report must represent your own investigation and reasoning.
points: Use teacher guidance and the actual descriptors, not a formulaic model report.
Present reproducible methods, transparent processing, evidence-based conclusions and specific evaluation.
Use a clean Chemistry data booklet in written examination preparation; practises here do not predict official grade boundaries.
example: Example: an evaluation gains value by explaining how a named limitation changes a measured result and why a concrete improvement reduces that effect. Merely listing “human error” does not explain its impact.
